papers.title_in_file: TOPOLOGICAL DATA ANALYSIS ON NOISY QUANTUM COMPUTERS
papers.version_note: The text is the ICLR 2024 conference version (arXiv 2209.09371v4, 19 Mar 2024), titled Topological data analysis on noisy quantum computers. The record's file name carries the earlier title, Exponential advantage on noisy quantum computers, with the same arXiv number. The abstract here matches the stored quotes. The footnote on p.25 and the acknowledgements say an earlier version had a flaw in the algorithm that was fixed with qubitization.
papers.what_it_is: A conference paper presenting NISQ-TDA, a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm that estimates normalized Betti numbers with a short-depth circuit, an error analysis, small hardware and noisy-simulation runs, and classical CMB-style experiments.

quotes: we present NISQ-TDA, a fully implemented end-to-end quantum machine learning algorithm needing only a short circuit-depth, that is applicable to high-dimensional classical data, and with provable asymptotic speedup for certain classes of problems.
existing.reader_inference: The hardware runs shown in Section 4 are Laplacian applications on an edge, a square and a cube, and the Betti-number estimates come from noisy simulations, so 'fully implemented' is the authors' wording and not a full end-to-end hardware run.

existing.note: The paper limits the claim elsewhere: it says it is unclear whether the algorithm gives substantial speedups on arbitrary data for Betti number estimation, and that it is unlikely to give quantum advantage for exact Betti numbers of clique complexes.
existing.value: The authors state that their algorithm still likely achieves exponential advantage over known classical approaches in efficiently answering whether a given simplicial complex has exponentially many holes. In Appendix A they also state that it is unclear whether NISQ-TDA will achieve substantial speedups on arbitrary data for Betti number estimation, and that NISQ-TDA is unlikely to achieve quantum advantage for estimation of exact Betti numbers of clique complexes.

assertions.value: The authors state that NISQ-TDA has three key components: a representation of the full boundary operator as a sum of Pauli operators, a quantum rejection sampling technique that projects onto the data-defined simplicial complex, and a stochastic rank estimation method that estimates the Betti numbers.
quotes: (a) an efficient representation of the full boundary operator as a sum of Pauli operators; (b) a quantum rejection sampling technique to project onto the data-defined simplicial complex; and (c) a stochastic rank estimation method to estimate the output signature Betti numbers.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the noisy simulations they chose complexes with large eigenvalue gaps and sufficiently many random vectors and shots, set the Chebyshev parameters so that the noise-free algorithm is almost exact, and take an error below 0.5 as tolerable since it rounds to the correct Betti number.
quotes: For this we chose complexes with large eigenvalue gaps, and sufficiently many random vectors and shots.
the error that can naturally be considered tolerable is 0.5, since any error less than 0.5 rounds to exactly the correct Betti number

assertions.value: The authors report that in noisy simulation with 8 vertices, degree 5 and noise level (0.001, 0.01), the estimated Betti number converges to about 1.84 against a true value of 2, and the variance falls as the number of random vectors increases.

We note that the mean converges to ∼ 1.84 (the true Betti number is β0 = 2) and, most importantly, the variance reduces as we increase nv.
assertions.reader_inference: The error of about 0.16 is below the 0.5 tolerance the authors set; this is one complex and one noise level.

assertions.value: The authors propose seven criteria for a useful quantum algorithm and assess NISQ-TDA against them: provable speedup is likely satisfied for certain instances, noise resilience seems satisfied as suggested by preliminary simulation and hardware results, and usefulness is likely satisfied.

papers.what_it_is: A position paper with a simulation study measuring an admission gate that confines LLM-agent self-evolution to the runtime harness in a synthetic credit-screening pipeline, with an EU AI Act mapping.

existing.note: The numbers are right. Section 10 limits the claim: the held-out history (Hval) is an interleaved half of the same pre-shift stream, labelled by the same deterministic rule as the gate pool, so zero false admissions is expected for any gated arm. The informative contrast is against the no-gate arm and on the post-shift held-out window. Section 7.1 also limits the no-gate harm: under the threshold family the no-gate arm's missed-flag rate stays near the oracle's; the loosening is a scope and structural effect.
existing.value: The authors report that the gated dual loop admitted 144 of 7,449 candidate changes, none of which worsened error on held-out history, and that the no-gate arm admitted 309 harmful changes and left missed flags above 10% in 49 of 90 runs; the authors state that the false-admission audit is weak by construction, because the gate half and the audit half are interleaved halves of the same pre-shift stream labelled by the same deterministic rule.
quotes: the gated dual loop admitted 144 of 7,449 candidate changes, none of which worsened error on held-out history
the same loops admitted 309 harmful changes and left missed flags above 10% in 49 of 90 runs
The false-admission audit is weak by construction.
